title: Justitia: Fair and Efficient Scheduling of Task-parallel LLM Agents with Selective Pampering
claim: Serving jobs in their fair completion order instead of sharing resources concurrently lowers average completion time without delaying any job.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left-to-right, shared time axis with colored resource blocks
description: Two side-by-side schematic Gantt-style area charts compare scheduling policies for two LLM agents, App-1 (yellow) and App-2 (blue). The y-axis is GPU block usage and the x-axis is time in minutes, from 0 to 8. Panel (a), Fair Sharing, has App-1 and App-2 running concurrently. App-1 takes the top half and finishes at 6 minutes. App-2 takes the bottom half, then the whole GPU after App-1 ends, and finishes at 8 minutes. Panel (b), Selective Pampering, runs App-1 alone on the full GPU until minute 3. App-2 then takes the full GPU until minute 8. App-1 therefore finishes earlier and App-2 finishes at the same time. The colors are flat and saturated. The eye goes first to the yellow block, which is wide in (a) and narrow in (b). Captions (a) and (b) sit below the panels.
caption: Given two competing LLM agents, serving them sequentially following their fair completion order, or selective pampering, can reduce the average completion time with no per-agent delay.
abstract: LLM agents, which often comprise parallel inference tasks, are commonly adopted to solve real-world problems. When serving such task-parallel LLM agents in shared GPU servers, the scheduler is expected to attain fast agent completion with guaranteed worst-case performance. For that objective, our insight is to selectively pampering agents based on their completion order under idealized fair-sharing. We design Justitia, a fair and also efficient scheduler for task-parallel LLM agents. Noticing that memory is prevalently a bottleneck in LLM serving, Justitia quantifies the true agent cost in a memory-centric manner. It also adopts a light-weight yet accurate method to predict agent costs. Finally, Justitia adopts a virtual-time based fair queuing algorithm to reduce the overall performance with guaranteed worst-case delay. We have implemented Justitia atop vLLM, and experimental results involving diverse agents show that it can substantially enhance the scheduling efficiency with fairness preserved.
